Fit, check and cross-validate the models of a table

Source: R/hazard-models.R
fit_hazard_models.Rd

Fits each model of a table built with build_hazard_models() to the same data with fit_hazard(), checks the sampling of each fit by one rule, and cross-validates each with loo_hazard(), leaving out the same unit. With kfold = TRUE each is also cross-validated by refitting, with kfold_hazard() and the same folds for every model. What it returns is what hazard_weights() and the functions that average models read.

Usage

fit_hazard_models(
  models,
  long,
  observation = c("interval", "continuous", "mixed"),
  unit = NULL,
  kfold = FALSE,
  K = NULL,
  rhat = 1.01,
  ess = 400,
  divergent = 0.001,
  ...
)

Arguments

models

A data frame, the table of models from build_hazard_models().

long

A data frame, the table of intervals at risk from build_hazard_data(), to which every model is fitted.

observation

A character string, how the failure times were observed, as in fit_hazard().

unit

An optional character string, the unit to leave out in cross-validation, as in loo_hazard(). NULL (the default) chooses it as loo_hazard() does.

kfold

A single logical value. TRUE also cross-validates each model by refitting, which takes one further fit per fold and model. Defaults to FALSE.

K

An optional single whole number, the number of folds when kfold is TRUE, as in kfold_hazard(). NULL (the default) gives one fold per unit. With fewer folds than units the units are assigned to folds at random, once for all the models; call set.seed() first to get the same folds, and the same estimates by refitting, again (see kfold_hazard()).

rhat

A single number above 1, the limit below which the Rhat of every parameter must lie. Defaults to 1.01.

ess

A single positive number, the limit above which the bulk and the tail effective sample size of every parameter must lie. Defaults to 400.

divergent

A single number from 0 to 1, the largest proportion of the draws that may come from divergent transitions. Defaults to 0.001.

...

Further arguments for every fit, passed to fit_hazard() and through it to brms::brm(), such as chains, iter, cores, seed and backend, or the priors that fit_hazard() takes. Those that brms::brm() takes are given to the refits of kfold = TRUE as well.

Value

A list with four elements. fits is a named list of the fitted models (brmsfit), without those that failed. loo is a named list of their cross-validation results from loo_hazard(). kfold is a named list of their results from kfold_hazard(), or NULL when kfold is FALSE. summary is a data frame with one row per model of the table: its name, failure-rate function and baseline; status ("fitted" or "failed") and, for a model that failed, the reason in message; the number of chains and draws; the largest rhat, the smallest ess_bulk and ess_tail and the number of divergent draws; rule_met, whether the sampling rule is met; rhat_group and ess_group, the largest Rhat and the smallest bulk or tail effective sample size over the group-level effects, outside the rule (NA for a model without them); elpd_loo with its standard error se_loo, and high_k, the number of units for which importance sampling cannot be trusted; elpd_kfold and se_kfold when kfold is TRUE; and seconds, the time the fit and its cross-validation took.

Details

The unit left out is settled before any model is fitted, as loo_hazard() chooses it, from the group-level terms of the models. Models that are compared must be cross-validated with the same unit, so the models of the table must share it; where their group-level terms would give different units, give unit.

A model whose fit fails does not stop the others. It is left out of the fits returned and is reported, with the reason, in the summary and in a warning. A fit that lost one of its chains is treated as failed: the diagnostics of the chains that are left would make it look complete.

The sampling rule is applied to the population-level coefficients and to the standard deviations and correlations of the group-level effects: the rank-normalised split-Rhat of each below rhat, the bulk and the tail effective sample size of each above ess, and at most the proportion divergent of the draws from divergent transitions. The three check different things: Rhat whether the chains agree, the effective sample sizes how precise the draws are, and the divergent transitions whether the sampler could reach every region; the rule is not called convergence, which is only the first of them. A fit that does not meet it is kept, since it is often the one to look at, and is marked in the summary and named in a warning. Whether to refit it, drop it or keep it is left to the user; zero divergent transitions and a rule that is met are not, by themselves, evidence that a model was sampled well. The limit of 400 on the effective sample sizes is 100 per chain for the four chains of the default (Vehtari et al. 2021); with more chains, raise it in proportion. The tolerance on divergent transitions exists so that a stray one does not fail a fit that is otherwise well sampled; a divergent transition is still evidence of a region the sampler could not enter, so where any remain, look at where those draws fall against the group-level standard deviations before reading the fit, and set divergent = 0 to refuse any.

The group-level effects themselves, such as the effect of each trial, are not part of the rule: a model with many levels would take its worst case over many parameters and exceed the limits by chance. They are reported beside it, as the largest Rhat and the smallest effective sample size over them, because the cross-validation by importance sampling, check_survival() and hazard_residuals() use each trial's fitted effect. The derived quantities do not: they are computed at the level of the population.

References

Vehtari, A., Gelman, A., Simpson, D., Carpenter, B. and Burkner, P.-C. (2021). Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: an improved Rhat for assessing convergence of MCMC. Bayesian Analysis 16, 667-718. doi:10.1214/20-BA1221

See also

hazard_weights() to weight the models, and average_tdt_ttl(), average_dctmax() and average_survival() to average them.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# a small ramping trial: 20 individuals warmed from 20 to 35 degrees over 60
# minutes and checked every minute, in two trials (see fit_hazard())
path   <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = c(0, 60), temp = c(20, 35))
checks <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = seq(0, 60, by = 1))
ind    <- data.frame(id = 1:20, path_id = "A", event = 1,
                     trial = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 10),
                     t_upper = sample(seq(10, 60, 10), 20, replace = TRUE))
long   <- build_hazard_data(ind, path, "interval", covariates = "trial",
                            checks = checks)

# the exponential failure rate with two baselines, each with a random intercept
# per trial on log a
models <- build_hazard_models("exp", c("mem", "weibull"),
                              dpar_formulas = list(loga = ~ 1 + (1 | trial)))
out <- fit_hazard_models(models, long, chains = 4, iter = 2000, cores = 4, seed = 1)
out$summary

# weight the models by how well each predicts a trial it was not fitted to, and
# average what is derived from them
weights <- hazard_weights(out$loo)
average_tdt_ttl(out$fits, weights, t_ref = 60)$sctmax
} # }
